Solving Molecular Epilepsy

What is needed now is a way to remove the parasitic resonances.

Based on the observation that, generally, the more complex a conjugated molecule is, the more resonance modes it possesses, it should therefore be possible to simplify the molecule. That is to say, reduce the complexity of the bonds in order to keep only the intended resonance modes.

Simplifying the Molecule

If we take the “Letter Envelope” structure and connect the two outputs of the NOR gates together, we obtain the 4 intended resonances plus the 2 expected parasitic resonances.

However, if we remove one of the connections, the molecule settles into a new, stable state without any parasites.

This results in a new structure called the “Barred Eight”. It acts as the functional equivalent of an AND logic gate.

Yet, more complex molecules require far more advanced transformations. It is not always as simple as removing a few bonds. At present, no general algorithm exists to automate this process. It remains an active area of research.

Quantum Couplers

Another approach is to filter the connections directly, since that is where the parasitic resonances originate.

Ideally, we would insert an intermediate filter molecule along the interconnect to ensure that both branches always maintain the exact same logical state.

However, such a purely chemical filter cannot work: because it must itself be open at both ends to connect into the circuit, it will inevitably develop the exact same parasitic resonances. We would simply be reproducing the initial problem.

To break this loop, we must rely on a different physical mechanism: quantum and electrostatic induction.

When two conjugated bonds are brought physically close to one another without touching, their -electron clouds interact across space. Just like electrical induction in classical physics, the alternating oscillation of electrons in one bond exerts an electrostatic and quantum exchange force on the neighbor:
* If one bond shifts into a double bond (-density), its local electric field repels or aligns the electron density of the adjacent bond.
* The two lines synchronize their states through the vacuum without sharing a single physical atom.

This wireless, contact-free bridge is what we call a Quantum Coupler or Coupler in short.

The coupling strength follows a strict physical scaling:
1. Shorter distance = stronger coupling: As the spatial gap narrows, the interaction strength increases drastically.
2. More bond pairs = higher efficiency: Chaining multiple coupled pairs in parallel reinforces the coherence.

By keeping the distance short enough and using enough parallel bond pairs, the synchronization efficiency can approach virtually 100%.

Typology of Couplers

Several physical geometries can be engineered:

  • Parallel Coupler: The simplest design to build. The two branches of the dual-rail interconnect are simply routed parallel and brought into close physical proximity.
  • Series Coupler: The molecular equivalent of a schematic of an electrical transformer. Two closed conjugated loops are placed side-by-side, transferring logic states purely through mutual resonance induction.
  • -Stacking Coupler (Face-to-Face): Instead of lying in the same 2D plane, conjugated rings are stacked directly on top of each other (via aromatic - stacking). This vertical configuration is exceptionally powerful for routing signals out of the plane and designing three-dimensional (3D) molecular circuits.

Beyond filtering parasites, couplers solve another major engineering hurdle: clean fan-out. They allow a single logic gate to cleanly broadcast its output to multiple gates without any physical wiring tangles or parasitic feedback.

Finally Success?

Yes! This time, the foundation holds.

Every essential building block has now been identified: from fundamental carbon junctions and resonance states to dual-rail interconnects, universal NOR logic, and parasitic-filtering couplers. The baseline theory is established, mathematically coherent, and fully functional!

“But wait…” the skeptic might object. “This is still just theory on paper, isn’t it? Some concepts seem radically counterintuitive. Where is the tangible physical prototype?”

First comes the blueprint, then comes the machine.

Historically, every monumental breakthrough in computing began as quiet derivations on a notepad. Alan Turing did not begin with silicon microchips, and quantum computing existed purely on chalkboards decades before the first qubit was frozen in a lab.

There are still vital, pioneering concepts waiting to be developed — and that is precisely what the upcoming posts will unpack.

Research is a journey of relentless patience; one must embrace the discipline of advancing one careful step at a time. Once the theoretical landscape is mapped, designing the physical architecture will become infinitely clearer.

Nevertheless, we must always keep a vigilant eye on physical reality — if only to ensure our feet remain firmly planted in the realm of the possible.

With our foundation established, this is the perfect moment to confront the toughest questions head-on. Let us address the most common scientific objections below!

Common Objections

  • “A molecule featuring a three-membered ring would be energetically unstable due to extreme ring strain.”

Quite right! If you ever read a headline announcing that a chemist has isolated a naked, three-membered conjugated carbon ring folded into an “envelope,” it would be nothing short of a miracle. The angle strain alone would tear it apart under ambient conditions.

However, remember our golden rule of interconnects: inserting an even number of carbon atoms into any bond preserves the exact logical identity of the circuit.

As a practical rule of thumb in molecular architecture: if a topology suffers from geometric strain or a lack of space, expand it by inserting pairs of carbon atoms.

By doing so, the bond angles relax toward the natural planar geometry of stable carbon. What begins as an overly strained toy graph eventually transitions into a thermodynamically stable, synthesizable molecule at ambient temperature and pressure.

Take our strained “Letter Envelope” model as a prime example:
1. In its minimal form, the envelope contains tight, highly strained three- and four-membered triangular cycles.
2. If we systematically insert two carbon atoms into the perimeter bonds of each strained loop, the tight angles open up.
3. The strained triangles gracefully blossom into stable five- and six-membered rings—yielding the planar polycyclic architecture known as Pyracylene ().

Pyracylene is not a theoretical fantasy: it is a real, well-documented molecule synthesized in organic chemistry laboratories (and famously observed as dynamic defects in graphene sheets under electron-beam irradiation).

It must be noted, however, that pyracylene has often been characterized by physical chemists as “borderline aromatic” (owing to the delicate balance between its aromatic benzene-like cores and its antiaromatic cyclooctatetraene-like peripheries).

Which brings us directly to the next objection…

  • “Several of these proposed topologies are non-aromatic, meaning their resonance structures are by no means equiprobable.”

This is a profound physical objection grounded in Hückel’s Rule of Aromaticity.

In physical chemistry, a planar, cyclic conjugated ring is exceptionally stable (aromatic) if it possesses delocalized -electrons (such as the 6 -electrons in benzene).

Conversely, when a ring contains -electrons (like cyclooctatetraene with 8 electrons), it enters an antiaromatic, electronically frustrated regime. To escape this high-energy penalty, the molecule undergoes a conformational distortion: it buckles out of the plane, warping into a non-planar geometry — much like a potato chip or a saddle.

Once planarity is broken:
* The overlap between adjacent atomic orbitals collapses.
* The continuous -cloud fragments into localized, unequal bond lengths.
* The resonance states split into widely different energy levels, destroying the uniform probabilistic branching required for clean logic transitions.

Constraining our computational designs strictly to Hückel-compliant rings would tend to cripple our architectures. Efficient logic circuits inevitably demand topologies that violate standard aromatic electron counts.

How do we overcome this energetic divergence? By enforcing planarity through mechanical tension.

If non-aromatic rings buckle because of electronic strain, we can physically prevent that distortion by anchoring the molecule within an external structural scaffold and tuning its perimeter tension — much like stretching and tuning a drumhead.

When clamped flat by external mechanical boundaries:
1. Out-of-plane buckling modes are geometrically suppressed.
2. Orbital overlap is uniformly restored across all carbon vertices.
3. The competing resonance configurations are forced into equipotential energy levels (energetic degeneracy).

Several realistic nanotechnology platforms could serve as this planarizing frame:

  • Perforated Graphene Frameworks: A pristine monolayer graphene sheet on a support can be nanolithographically patterned with nanopores. Molecular logic units can then be suspended across these nanometer-scale voids, anchored at the edges using natural heteroatomic “clips” — specifically divalent oxygen bridges (, ether linkages) or trivalent nitrogen junctions (, tertiary amine nodes) standard in organic synthesis.
  • Protein and Enzyme Scaffolds: In biological systems, enzymes frequently force substrate molecules into chemically unnatural, high-energy planar transition states through rigid hydrophobic binding pockets. Supramolecular protein cages could act as macroscopic templates, mechanically clamping carbon logic circuits into the required planar topology.
  • Atomically Flat Substrates (On-Surface Template Synthesis): A proven technique in modern molecular electronics consists of depositing molecular precursors onto ultra-flat crystalline surfaces—such as gold or thin insulating layers of sodium chloride () on copper. Strong interfacial van der Waals forces act as an electrostatic press, physically flattening the carbon backbone against the substrate and completely quenching out-of-plane buckling modes.
  • Covalent Organic Frameworks (COFs): Rather than manually carving cavities into existing materials, one can synthesize self-assembling 2D crystalline polymer sheets known as COFs. These frameworks naturally form rigid, highly ordered porous networks. Molecular logic units can be engineered as modular tiles that integrate seamlessly into the lattice pores, leveraging the surrounding network as a built-in, thermally stable rigid chassis.
  • Nanotube Suspension Tensors: Suspending the molecular network between parallel single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) allows for active, dynamic mechanical tuning. By applying controlled electrostatic fields or piezo-actuation across the nanotube anchors, the external tension on the circuit can be adjusted in real time—the nanomechanical equivalent of tuning pegs on a guitar.

Admittedly, experimental optimal scaffolding techniques remains an open frontier. What matters at this stage is that viable physical pathways exist: there are no thermodynamics violation; we simply need to engineer the boundary constraints.

  • “Larger molecular networks would suffer from rapid environmental decoherence in any realistic, noisy medium.”

  • “How are the physical inputs and outputs concretely interfaced with the rest of the circuit?”

Speculations & Wild Thoughts

  • Could an epileptic seizure be a molecular circuit bug?
    In the brain, synapses are packed with aromatic carbon rings. What if they use π-electron resonance for ultra-fast signaling? If a tiny molecular coupler stretches just a little too far, it breaks. In our circuits, that single broken coupler unleashes parasitic resonances that invade the entire network. Could an epileptic seizure simply be this exact bug happening at a biological scale — a runaway chain reaction of molecular noise that locks millions of synapses into a synchronized freeze?

  • Beyond π-Logic:
    Back in 2006, M. H. van der Veen showed that electrons jumping inside conjugated molecules could act as logic gates (“π-Logic”). But they relied on light and lasers to switch them on and off. My approach takes the next step: no lasers, no external triggers. By letting the bonds resonate naturally the molecule computes natively and reversibly on its own.

  • Penrose, Paramecia, and Sub-Cellular Computing:
    A single-celled paramecium has no neurons, no synapses, and no brain. Yet, it swims, avoids obstacles, hunts for food, mates, and learns from its environment. As Sir Roger Penrose and Stuart Hameroff famously wondered: if a neuron is just a binary on/off switch, how does a brainless, single cell compute complex behaviors? The answer may lie within: a single neuron is not a simple bit—it is already a complete molecular supercomputer. Information processing does not start at the neural network level; it is fundamentally driven by the quantum resonance of conjugated -systems inside the cell’s cytoskeleton.

  • The Slime Mold Paradox (Mazes Without a Brain):
    The slime mold (Physarum polycephalum) is a single giant cell without a nervous system. Yet, it famously solves mazes, re-creates the optimal topology of Tokyo’s railway network, and remembers past experiences. Standard biology describes this as passive chemical diffusion. But what if the cell’s internal protein lattice is actively executing logic? A molecule can compute by global wave relaxation through boundary conditions. The slime mold might be doing the exact same thing on a macroscopic scale: solving optimization problems not by stepping through lines of code, but through the natural physics of conjugated resonance.

  • Plant Memory and the Carbon Web:
    Plants lack a nervous system, yet the sensitive plant (Mimosa pudica) can learn to ignore harmless falls and retain that memory for weeks. Trees synchronize resource distribution across vast fungal networks and anticipate daily solar cycles long before dawn. Rather than relying on fragile electrical action potentials, plants may process and store environmental information directly within their rich architecture of aromatic compounds and carbon lattices. Life spent nearly four billion years computing with carbon bonds before it ever evolved a brain. Neurons might be high-speed cables connecting nature’s ancient, organic computers.

Solving the Rigidity Deadlock

Let us now step back and examine molecules in their complete, closed-form topologies—where every single carbon atom of the network is explicitly accounted for, with no dangling bonds or hidden external leads.

Consider the resonance manifold of a relatively simple structure: the Double Honeycomb (naphthalene-like fused rings).

Code 
# Create a conjugated carbon molecule
mol1 = CarbonMolecule("Double Honeycomb")

# Add atoms
c1_1 = mol1.add_atom(x=-0.25, y=1)
c1_2 = mol1.add_atom(x=0.25, y=1)
c1_3 = mol1.add_atom(x=-0.5, y=0.5)
c1_4 = mol1.add_atom(x=0.5, y=0.5)
c1_5 = mol1.add_atom(x=-0.25, y=0)
c1_6 = mol1.add_atom(x=0.25, y=0)
c1_7 = mol1.add_atom(x=-0.5, y=-0.5)
c1_8 = mol1.add_atom(x=0.5, y=-0.5)
c1_9 = mol1.add_atom(x=-0.25, y=-1)
c1_10 = mol1.add_atom(x=0.25, y=-1)

# Add bonds
b1_1 = mol1.add_bond(c1_1, c1_2, order="single", label="A", role="input")
b1_2 = mol1.add_bond(c1_2, c1_4, order="single")
b1_3 = mol1.add_bond(c1_1, c1_3, order="single")
b1_4 = mol1.add_bond(c1_3, c1_5, order="single")
b1_5 = mol1.add_bond(c1_4, c1_6, order="single")
b1_6 = mol1.add_bond(c1_5, c1_6, order="single")
b1_7 = mol1.add_bond(c1_5, c1_7, order="single")
b1_8 = mol1.add_bond(c1_6, c1_8, order="single")
b1_9 = mol1.add_bond(c1_7, c1_9, order="single")
b1_10 = mol1.add_bond(c1_8, c1_10, order="single")
b1_11 = mol1.add_bond(c1_9, c1_10, order="single", label="B", role="output")

all_resonances = mol1.resonance()

for i, res_mol in enumerate(all_resonances):
    res_mol.draw()

Now, let us isolate and observe the resulting resonance truth table strictly across boundary bonds and :

Code 
CarbonMolecule.resonance_table(all_resonances)

Designating bond as an input and bond as an output reveals something remarkable:

When input is held at state “0” (single bond), output is no longer clamped to a single, rigid outcome. Instead, it can naturally manifest in two distinct states: “0” or “1”.

This is an immensely encouraging breakthrough. This internal branching is precisely the missing degree of freedom that eluded us when analyzing isolated junctions!

And this is by no means an isolated anomaly. The overwhelming majority of closed-form conjugated networks exhibit this rich internal multiplicity. All it took was shifting the perspective: stepping back to appreciate the entire molecular forest rather than obsessing over an isolated junction tree.

However, this breakthrough carries a profound theoretical consequence: deterministic certainty dissolves here.

Because a single input state maps to multiple admissible physical configurations, classical boolean determinism can no longer describe the computation. We are inevitably forced to expand our mathematical framework into the domain of statistics.

Probabilistic Bits (p-bits)

Probabilistic bits provide a robust mathematical framework for encoding and processing information. By applying this formalism to carbon-carbon bonds, we can natively capture the stochastic nature of chemical systems and open up new frontiers in molecular computing.

Think of a coin toss. Once flipped, the coin can land on tails (state “0”) or heads (state “1”).

With a fair coin, there is an equal probability — a 50% chance—of landing on state “0” and a 50% chance of landing on state “1”.

Mathematically, we formulate probabilistic bits using the same transition matrices introduced earlier. The only operational difference lies in the continuous values of the matrix elements rather than discrete binary indicators.

  • A fair coin:
Code 
display_inline("Fair", "=", random.to_katex(show_labels=True))

The first element quantifies the probability of observing a “0”; the second element quantifies the probability of observing a “1”.

We could also bias the coin so that it carries a one-in-four chance (25%) of landing on “0”, and a three-in-four chance (75%) of landing on “1”.

  • A biased coin:
Code 
biased = TransitionMatrix([
    [0.25, 0.75]
])

display_inline("Biased", "=", biased.to_katex(show_labels=True))

The limiting boundary case occurs when there is a 0% chance of being in one state and a 100% chance of being in the other. Under these conditions, deterministic certainty is recovered, and the probabilistic bit collapses back into a classical boolean bit ( or ).

Any transition matrix is physically and computationally admissible in our model if it satisfies three structural properties:

  1. Bounded Probabilities: Every individual element must lie strictly within the closed interval (no negative or super-unitary probabilities).
  2. Conservation of Probability: For any accessible state, the elements along the row must sum to exactly 1 (100% of the probability distribution, ensuring no leakage into unmodeled states).
  3. Forbidden Inputs: If an input configuration is topologically or chemically forbidden by the molecular network, all elements along that row sum to exactly 0, acting as an algebraic filter that rejects unphysical states.

We can now derive the complete transition matrix for the Double Honeycomb molecule (with bond 𝐴 as an input and bond 𝐵 as an output):

Code 
doubleHoneycomb = TransitionMatrix.from_resonances(all_resonances)

display_inline("DoubleHoneycomb", "=", doubleHoneycomb.to_katex(show_labels=True))

Examining the matrix reveals an interesting hybrid behavior:
* When input is held at “0”, output behaves as a fair coin (), exhibiting true probabilistic branching.
* When input is held at “1”, output collapses into a deterministic boolean bit strictly clamped to “0” ().

Solving the Universal Logic Deadlock

At first glance, one might worry that all these fractional probability matrices are merely drifting further away from our original goal: constructing deterministic, universal logic gates.

Intuitively, however, a compelling hypothesis emerges: what happens if we mirror and fuse two identical junctions together?

Because both halves share identical resonance tables, connecting their boundaries should not induce chaotic frustration or instability. Instead, mutual geometric symmetry could act as an internal stabilizer, potentially maintaining deterministic transitions. It was by no means guaranteed, but it was an avenue demanding exploration.

This hunch led to an astonishing breakthrough when fusing two triangular junctions face-to-face.

Code 
# Create a conjugated carbon molecule
mol = CarbonMolecule("2X Triangular Junction")

# Add atoms
c2_1 = mol.add_atom(x=-0.8, y=0.5)
c2_2 = mol.add_atom(x=0.3, y=0.5, visible=False)
c2_3 = mol.add_atom(x=-0.8, y=-0.5)

c2_5 = mol.add_atom(x=-0.3, y=0)

c2_7 = mol.add_atom(x=1.8, y=0.5)

c2_9 = mol.add_atom(x=1.8, y=-0.5)
c2_10 = mol.add_atom(x=0.7, y=-0.5, visible=False)
c2_11 = mol.add_atom(x=1.3, y=0)

# Add bonds
b2_1 = mol.add_bond(c2_1, c2_2, order="single", label="A")

b2_3 = mol.add_bond(c2_5, c2_6, order="single", label="C")

# Draw with Schemdraw

The resulting network forms a symmetric structure called the “Letter Envelope”. Here are its 4 fundamental resonance structures:

Code 
# Create a conjugated carbon molecule
mol = CarbonMolecule("Letter Envelope")

# Add atoms
c2_1 = mol.add_atom(x=-0.8, y=0.5)
c2_2 = mol.add_atom(x=0.8, y=0.5)
c2_3 = mol.add_atom(x=-0.3, y=0)
c2_4 = mol.add_atom(x=0.3, y=0)
c2_5 = mol.add_atom(x=-0.8, y=-0.5)
c2_6 = mol.add_atom(x=0.8, y=-0.5)

# Add bonds
b2_1 = mol.add_bond(c2_1, c2_2, order="single", label="A")
b2_2 = mol.add_bond(c2_1, c2_5, order="single", label="E1")
b2_3 = mol.add_bond(c2_2, c2_6, order="single", label="E2")
b2_4 = mol.add_bond(c2_1, c2_3, order="single", label="D1")
b2_5 = mol.add_bond(c2_2, c2_4, order="single", label="D2")
b2_6 = mol.add_bond(c2_3, c2_4, order="single", label="C")
b2_7 = mol.add_bond(c2_3, c2_5, order="single", label="F1")
b2_8 = mol.add_bond(c2_4, c2_6, order="single", label="F2")
b2_9 = mol.add_bond(c2_5, c2_6, order="single", label="B")

all_resonances = mol.resonance()

for i, res_mol in enumerate(all_resonances):
    res_mol.draw()

Now, let us examine the global resonance table across all labeled bonds:

Code 
CarbonMolecule.resonance_table(all_resonances)

If we assign and as inputs and inspect bond as the output, we recover our familiar XNOR gate. Given that both halves are triangular junctions, this is reassuring, but not groundbreaking.

Now, shift your focus to bond instead.

Look at the truth table for :
* evaluates to “1” if and only if both inputs and are “0”.
* In all other configurations, evaluates strictly to “0”.

This is the exact, canonical definition of a NOR gate !

Not only is the NOR gate a universal logic primitive capable of synthesizing any classical computational function (NAND, AND, OR, XOR), but this molecular geometry natively provides two symmetric outputs for the price of one ( and yield identical values, offering built-in fan-out).

The universal logic deadlock is officially broken. We now possess a tangible molecular blueprint for universal boolean computation etched directly into a conjugated carbon skeleton.

Dual-Rail Interconnects

Now that we have successfully synthesized a universal NOR gate within a closed-form molecule, a critical architectural question emerges: how do we chain these logic gates together to build complex circuits?

The naive approach—connecting functional blocks via a single, isolated carbon bond as we did with elementary junctions—is no longer viable.

Examine what happens when we open one of the inputs of our “Letter Envelope” molecule: it does not terminate in a single dangling bond, but rather in a symmetric pair of coupled branches. Due to the internal geometry of the resonance network, these two parallel branches are physically locked together—they will always carry the exact same logical state simultaneously.

Code 
# Create a conjugated carbon molecule
mol = CarbonMolecule("Letter Envelope")

# Add atoms
c_1a = mol.add_atom(x=-0.8, y=0.5)
c_1b = mol.add_atom(x=-0.4, y=0.7, visible=False)
c_2a = mol.add_atom(x=0.8, y=0.5)
c_2b = mol.add_atom(x=0.4, y=0.7, visible=False)
c_3 = mol.add_atom(x=-0.3, y=0)
c_4 = mol.add_atom(x=0.3, y=0)
c_5 = mol.add_atom(x=-0.8, y=-0.5)
c_6 = mol.add_atom(x=0.8, y=-0.5)

# Add bonds
b_1a = mol.add_bond(c_1a, c_1b, order="single")
b_1b = mol.add_bond(c_2a, c_2b, order="single")
b_2 = mol.add_bond(c_1a, c_5, order="single")

all_resonances = mol.resonance()

for i, res_mol in enumerate(all_resonances):
    res_mol.draw()

The engineering solution is as elegant as it is direct: instead of routing a single line, we route both branches in parallel.

Code 
with schemdraw.Drawing() as d:
    d.config(fontsize=12, unit=2.5)

    # 1. Top XNOR gate (Inputs: A, B -> Output: D)
    top_gate = d.add(logic.Xnor().right().label("XNOR 1", loc="top"))
    
    # Lead wire and label for Input B (top pin of top gate)
    d.add(elm.Line().left(2.5).at(top_gate.in1).label("B", loc="left"))
    
    # Output wire and label for Output D
    d.add(elm.Line().right(1.5).at(top_gate.out).label("D", loc="right"))

    # 2. Bottom XNOR gate (Inputs: A, C -> Output: E)
    # Positioned neatly below the first gate
    bottom_gate = d.add(
        logic.Xnor().right().at((top_gate.absanchors["in1"][0], top_gate.absanchors["in1"][1] - 3.5))
        .label("XNOR 2", loc="bottom")
    )

    # Lead wire and label for Input C (bottom pin of bottom gate)
    d.add(elm.Line().left(2.5).at(bottom_gate.in2).label("C", loc="left"))
    
    # Output wire and label for Output E
    d.add(elm.Line().right(1.5).at(bottom_gate.out).label("E", loc="right"))

    # 3. Shared Input A routing (Fan-out to top_gate.in2 and bottom_gate.in1)
    # Lead line from the left
    mid_y = (top_gate.in2[1] + bottom_gate.in1[1]) / 2.0
    input_A = d.add(elm.Line().right(1.2).at((top_gate.in1[0] - 2.5, mid_y)).label("A", loc="left"))
    
    # Route branch up into top gate (in2)
    d.add(elm.Wire("-|").at(input_A.end).to(top_gate.in2))

    # Route branch down into bottom gate (in1)
    d.add(elm.Wire("-|").at(input_A.end).to(bottom_gate.in1))

In modern computer architecture, this paradigm is well known as dual-rail logic (or differential signaling). In our molecular context, information is not propagated across a single wire, but through a two-lane conjugated pathway.

Notice that the top branch incorporates two additional carbon atoms compared to the bottom branch. This specific geometric offset is not strictly mandatory: as long as we insert an even number of carbon atoms along the conjugated pathway, the wire remains logically equivalent and non-inverting (a pure identity interconnect).

Conversely, inserting an odd number of carbon atoms into each branch introduces a parity shift in the alternating double/single bonds. This naturally inverts the logical state, effectively transforming the interconnect itself into a built-in NOT gate without requiring any additional circuit components.

Furthermore, the upper branch was chosen to represent the value of A. However, the lower branch would have been equally suitable; they always have the same value anyway.

Cascading Parasitic Resonance (Molecular Epilepsy)

The path now seems crystal clear: with a universal NOR gate and dual-rail interconnects, it is theoretically possible to chain together as many logic gates as the architecture demands. The logic is universal, mathematically sound, and geometrically elegant.

The foundation appears to be firmly laid. All that remains is to build upward.

Yet, as the very first bricks are set into place, the entire structure shakes violently and collapses to the ground.

What on earth just happened?

In any realistic digital circuit, signals do not merely propagate along a single, open pipeline. Functional processors are inherently dense, intertwined networks featuring branching, reconverging paths, and feedback loops.

Every time we fuse two carbon networks together, we do not simply create an abstract connection: we synthesize a single, larger macro-molecule

To construct a circuit of even modest complexity, one must inevitably: open and interconnect two separate bonds within the very same molecule.

And that is where the physics turns against us.

Opening a single bond is well-behaved: the dangling bonds remain strictly synchronized, faithfully executing the truth table.

However, the moment we expose a second connection port on that same molecular envelope, an insidious form of crosstalk emerges. The extended boundary conditions crack open the state space, allowing four rogue, parasitic resonance modes to settle into the manifold.

Code 
# Create a conjugated carbon molecule
mol = CarbonMolecule("Letter Envelope")

# Add atoms

c_1b = mol.add_atom(x=-0.4, y=0.7, visible=False)
c_2a = mol.add_atom(x=0.8, y=0.5)

c_6a = mol.add_atom(x=0.8, y=-0.5)
c_6b = mol.add_atom(x=0.4, y=-0.7, visible=False)

# Add bonds
b_1a = mol.add_bond(c_1a, c_1b, order="single")
b_1b = mol.add_bond(c_2a, c_2b, order="single")

all_resonances = mol.resonance()

for i, res_mol in enumerate(all_resonances):
    res_mol.draw()

After connecting the two open bonds together, two unauthorized states will remain.

These two unauthorized states do not remain polite, isolated local defects. Because the molecular -system is continuous, these parasitic modes propagate unimpeded throughout the entire network, corrupting every gate in their path like a wildfire.

In formal physical terms, this catastrophic breakdown is known as Cascading Parasitic Resonance.

A far more striking and visceral name for it, however, is “Molecular Epilepsy.”

This is not a mere poetic metaphor. If one were to construct an artificial neural network physically embodied in conjugated carbon molecules, this is hypothetically the exact pathology that would emerge: the moment an internal feedback loop loses its structural constraints, a runaway parasitic resonance takes over the network, mimicking the hypersynchronous seizure activity observed in biological neural tissue.

In other words, the machine ceases to calculate. It convulses.

“An atom has no identity of its own. Only a function within the whole.”
— Professor Alvin

Click to see library imports

Could it be that the capacity to process and manipulate information is woven into the very fabric of molecules?

We now turn to explore the untapped potential of atoms and their chemical bonds to create sophisticated computational systems.

Chemical Bonds

The molecules of primary interest here are those with carbon atoms, owing to their fundamental ability to form four covalent bonds. While other elements, such as silicon, share this tetravalent property, carbon will serve as our foundational element throughout this blog due to its central role in organic chemistry.

Carbon atoms do not dance alone in this molecular choreography; they interact with other key elements, notably hydrogen (which typically forms one bond), oxygen (which forms two), and nitrogen (which forms three). Combined with carbon, these elements constitute the elemental building blocks of a rich and complex chemistry:

Code 
with schemdraw.Drawing() as d:
    d.config(fontsize=14)

    # --- Row 1: Single Bond (H - C) ---
    d += elm.Line(lw=2).at((0, 0)).to((2.5, 0))
    # Draw dots AFTER the line so they sit cleanly on top
    d += elm.Dot(radius=0.45).at((0, 0)).color('#1E88E5').fill('#E3F2FD').label('H', loc='center', color='black')
    d += elm.Dot(radius=0.45).at((2.5, 0)).color('#424242').fill('#E0E0E0').label('C', loc='center', color='black')
    d += elm.Label().at((3.6, 0)).label('Hydrogen – Carbon: 1 bond', halign='left', valign='center')

    # --- Row 2: Double Bond (O = C) ---
    d += elm.Line(lw=4.5).at((0, -2)).to((2.5, -2))
    d += elm.Dot(radius=0.45).at((0, -2)).color('#E53935').fill('#FFCDD2').label('O', loc='center', color='black')
    d += elm.Dot(radius=0.45).at((2.5, -2)).color('#424242').fill('#E0E0E0').label('C', loc='center', color='black')
    d += elm.Label().at((3.6, -2)).label('Oxygen – Carbon: 2 bonds', halign='left', valign='center')

    # --- Row 3: Triple Bond (N ≡ C) ---
    d += elm.Line(lw=7.5).at((0, -4)).to((2.5, -4))
    d += elm.Dot(radius=0.45).at((0, -4)).color('#43A047').fill('#C8E6C9').label('N', loc='center', color='black')
    d += elm.Dot(radius=0.45).at((2.5, -4)).color('#424242').fill('#E0E0E0').label('C', loc='center', color='black')
    d += elm.Label().at((3.6, -4)).label('Nitrogen – Carbon: 3 bonds', halign='left', valign='center')

Chemical bonds can naturally be harnessed to encode discrete binary states. For instance, a single bond between two carbon atoms can be defined as representing a state “0”, whereas a double bond can represent a state “1”.
We will not be using triple bonds here for reasons that will soon become clear.

Orbitals

Where do these specific bond valencies and spatial bond angles actually originate? The answer lies within the concept of atomic and molecular orbitals.

An orbital is a region of space around an atomic nucleus where the probability of finding an electron is highest. These regions are governed by mathematical wavefunctions—the direct solutions to the fundamental equations of quantum mechanics.

These orbitals exhibit varied geometries and scales, classified by sets of quantum numbers. The , , , and subshells, for instance, possess distinct spatial shapes that directly dictate how atoms bond. The -orbitals, with their characteristic dumbbell-shaped lobes oriented along Cartesian axes, are critically important for the formation of the covalent bonds prevalent in organic and aromatic architectures.

When atomic orbitals interact, they combine to produce hybrid orbitals, which ultimately govern the geometry of molecular structures.
For carbon:
* hybridization yields four single bonds symmetrically arranged in a three-dimensional tetrahedron (with angles).
* hybridization yields planar geometries ( angles), creating the structural framework for double bonds.
* hybridization yields linear geometries ( angles), establishing triple bonds.

Delocalization in Conjugated Systems

In conjugated and aromatic systems, electrons are free to delocalize across multiple atomic centers:

Take benzene as the quintessential example: the (pi) electrons that form the alternating double bonds are not strictly bound between adjacent pairs of carbon atoms. Instead, they form a continuous, delocalized electron cloud extending uniformly over the entire hexagonal ring.

This resonance phenomenon is a direct physical manifestation of quantum mechanics. It demonstrates how quantum entities occupy coherent superpositions rather than classical point-like positions.
To be clear: these are not localized particles mechanically “spinning in circles” around the ring, but rather an integrated, collective electronic state.

This delocalization is far from a mere theoretical curiosity; it carries profound practical implications. The continuous nature of the -cloud dictates the molecule’s chemical stability, its electronic band structure, its charge transport capabilities, and its optical response.

The Initial Spark: Trivalent Carbon Nodes

The computational potential of a carbon atom bonded to three adjacent atoms ( planar center) is particularly intriguing. Such an atom acts naturally as a branching node within a molecular graph, where each chemical bond functions as a logical interconnect.

To satisfy carbon’s fundamental tetravalence (four total bonds), exactly one of these three bonds can be a double bond at any given moment, while the remaining two must be single bonds. Consequently, the local bond configuration at this trivalent node can manifest in three mutually exclusive states:

Code 
# Create a conjugated 3-carbon node
mol = CarbonMolecule("TrivalentNode")

# Add 4 atoms (Center node + 3 branches)
c_center = mol.add_atom(x=0, y=0, isotope="C12")
c_top    = mol.add_atom(x=0, y=0.5, isotope="C12", visible=False, label="C1")
c_left   = mol.add_atom(x=-0.435, y=-0.4, isotope="C12", visible=False, label="C2")
c_right  = mol.add_atom(x=0.435, y=-0.4, isotope="C12", visible=False, label="C3")

# Add bonds (one double bond, two single bonds)
b1 = mol.add_bond(c_center, c_top, order="double", label="A")
b2 = mol.add_bond(c_center, c_left, order="single", label="B")
b3 = mol.add_bond(c_center, c_right, order="single", label="C")

# Draw with Schemdraw
mol.draw()

# Second resonance
b1.order = "single"
b2.order = "double"

mol.draw()

# Third resonance
b2.order = "single"
b3.order = "double"

mol.draw()

This set of configurations corresponds directly to the resonance structures of the molecular node.

We can express this physical valence constraint through the following Boolean relation:

Or represented as an equivalent logic circuit:

Code 
with schemdraw.Drawing() as d:
    d.config(fontsize=12, unit=2.5)

    # 1. Gates: 3-input XOR (top) and 3-input AND (bottom)
    # inputs=3 exposes anchors: in1, in2, in3
    xor3 = d.add(logic.Xor(inputs=3).right().at((4, 2)))
    and3 = d.add(logic.And(inputs=3).right().at((4, 0)))

    # 2. Final 2-input XOR combining both branches
    xor_final = d.add(logic.Xor().right().at((6, 1)))
    d.add(elm.Wire('|-').at(xor3.out).to(xor_final.in1))
    d.add(elm.Wire('|-').at(and3.out).to(xor_final.in2))

    # Output line constrained to "1"
    d.add(elm.Line().right(1.5).at(xor_final.out).label('"1"', loc='right'))

    # 3. Clean input bus routing for A, B, C
    # Input A (top pin: in1)
    d.add(elm.Line().left(3).at(xor3.in1).label('A', loc='left'))
    d.add(elm.Dot().at((xor3.in1[0]-0.5,xor3.in1[1])))
    d.add(elm.Wire('|-').at((xor3.in1[0]-0.5,xor3.in1[1])).to(and3.in1))

    # Input B (middle pin: in2)
    d.add(elm.Line().left(3).at(xor3.in2).label('B', loc='left'))
    d.add(elm.Dot().at((xor3.in2[0]-1.0,xor3.in2[1])))
    d.add(elm.Wire('|-').at((xor3.in2[0]-1.0,xor3.in2[1])).to(and3.in2))

    # Input C (bottom pin: in3)
    d.add(elm.Line().left(3).at(xor3.in3).label('C', loc='left'))
    d.add(elm.Dot().at((xor3.in3[0]-1.5,xor3.in3[1])))
    d.add(elm.Wire('|-').at((xor3.in3[0]-1.5,xor3.in3[1])).to(and3.in3))

Given that combining an AND operation with an XOR operation provides the functional completeness required to synthesize a universal NAND gate, we immediately see that all the necessary mathematical ingredients for universal computation are naturally embedded within the valence rules of a single carbon node.

There is clearly substantial potential here — the challenge now is simply learning how to tame and harness it…

It was precisely this early, encouraging realization that provided the initial momentum to dive deeper into the exploration of conjugated carbon circuits.

Skeletal Structures

After systematically testing every possible combination, it became clear that only two fundamental types of connections are strictly necessary:

Because the presence of hydrogen atoms can be unambiguously deduced by counting the number of carbon-carbon bonds, we can streamline our drawings by adopting skeletal structures.

Notice the subtle yet crucial differences compared to standard skeletal notation:

The convention of drawing double bonds offset to one specific side of a ring — even when that -bond is physically shared across two fused rings — is far too crude and misleading. Particularly when looking for symmetries.

Dotted carbon atoms should also be drawn. As we move forward, we will be analyzing the resonance manifolds of highly intricate molecular networks. Sometimes the lines get curvy and it isn’t clear anymore where the atoms are.

The last thing we need is to bog down our analysis with ambiguous notations. Clarity is paramount.

Junction Resonances

Let us now explore the resonance manifolds (Kekulé states) of various molecular junctions.

We begin with a simple elementary case: the linear junction.

Code 
# Create Molecule
mol1 = CarbonMolecule("linear junction")

# Add atoms
c1 = mol1.add_atom(x=0, y=0, visible=False)
c2 = mol1.add_atom(x=0.5, y=0.5, visible=True)
c3 = mol1.add_atom(x=1, y=0.0, visible=False)

# Add bonds
b1 = mol1.add_bond(c1, c2, order="single", label="A")
b2 = mol1.add_bond(c2, c3, order="single", label="B")

# Draw with Schemdraw
mol1.draw()

Note: in junctions we can see bonds that end without an atom. This simply illustrates that the atom is connected to another one outside the page. Obviously, in our physical reality, a bond can never end in a void.

This junction exhibits two distinct resonance modes:

Code 
all_resonances = mol1.resonance()

for i, res_mol in enumerate(all_resonances):
    res_mol.draw()

We can compile these resonance states into a truth table where each row corresponds to one of the possible resonance configurations.

Code 
CarbonMolecule.resonance_table(all_resonances)

As we can observe, the state of is always the exact inverse of . This yields a truth table functionally identical to a classical NOT gate.

You can practice by sketching an arbitrary simple junction and determining its allowed resonance modes. It is a remarkably effective exercise for developing a physical feel for how these molecular networks behave.

Through this exercise, you will quickly encounter the triangular junction:

Code 
# Create Molecule
mol2 = CarbonMolecule("triangular junction")

# Add atoms
c1 = mol2.add_atom(x=0, y=0.75, visible=False)
c2 = mol2.add_atom(x=-0.75, y=-0.75, visible=False)
c3 = mol2.add_atom(x=0.75, y=-0.75, visible=False)
c4 = mol2.add_atom(x=0, y=0.25, visible=True)
c5 = mol2.add_atom(x=-0.25, y=-0.25, visible=True)
c6 = mol2.add_atom(x=0.25, y=-0.25, visible=True)

# Add bonds
b1 = mol2.add_bond(c1, c4, order="single", label="A")
b2 = mol2.add_bond(c2, c5, order="single", label="B")
b3 = mol2.add_bond(c3, c6, order="single", label="C")
b4 = mol2.add_bond(c4, c5, order="single")
b5 = mol2.add_bond(c5, c6, order="single")
b6 = mol2.add_bond(c6, c4, order="single")

# Draw with Schemdraw
mol2.draw()

It features four resonance modes:

Code 
all_resonances = mol2.resonance()

for i, res_mol in enumerate(all_resonances):
    res_mol.draw()

And here is the resulting truth table:

Code 
CarbonMolecule.resonance_table(all_resonances)

Notice that this table directly mirrors the behavior of a XNOR gate.

Now let us examine a slightly more intricate topology: the “H” junction.

Code 
# Create Molecule
mol3 = CarbonMolecule('"H" junction')

# Add atoms
c1 = mol3.add_atom(x=0, y=0.5, visible=False)
c2 = mol3.add_atom(x=0, y=-0.5, visible=False)
c3 = mol3.add_atom(x=0.5, y=0, visible=True)
c4 = mol3.add_atom(x=1, y=0, visible=True)
c5 = mol3.add_atom(x=1.5, y=0.5, visible=False)
c6 = mol3.add_atom(x=1.5, y=-0.5, visible=False)

# Add bonds
b1 = mol3.add_bond(c1, c3, order="single", label="A", role="input")
b2 = mol3.add_bond(c2, c3, order="single", label="B", role="input")
b3 = mol3.add_bond(c5, c4, order="single", label="C", role="input")
b4 = mol3.add_bond(c6, c4, order="single", label="D", role="output")
b5 = mol3.add_bond(c3, c4, order="single")

# Draw with Schemdraw
mol3.draw()

This junction possesses five resonance modes:

Code 
all_resonances = mol3.resonance()

for i, res_mol in enumerate(all_resonances):
    res_mol.draw()

And here is the resulting table:

Code 
CarbonMolecule.resonance_table(all_resonances)

Note that the table above does not correspond to any standard logic gate. Some row values are missing. So even a combination of classical boolean gates wouldn’t be able to represent this logic. The vast majority of molecular topologies behave this way.

Forbidden Transitions

We need a consistent way to handle impossible or missing input configurations in our transition matrices. We achieve this by setting all elements along the corresponding row to 0 (representing an unreachable or dead-end state).

For the “H” junction above, if we define , , and as inputs and as the output, the transition matrix representing this molecular circuit becomes:

Code 
hjunction = TransitionMatrix.from_resonances(all_resonances)

display_inline("Hjunction", "=", hjunction.to_katex(show_labels=True))

Because certain rows sum to less than 1 (zero, in fact), the matrix becomes sub-stochastic. This should not be a cause for concern: it is not a defect or a bug in a Markov chain.

We can compute with such matrices seamlessly. Simply think of an all-zero row as an algebraic placeholder indicating that a given input combination is physically forbidden by the molecule’s valency rules.

The Junction Snag

Up to this point, our exploration has yielded two functional primitives: a NOT gate (from the linear junction) and a XNOR gate (from the triangular junction).

While promising, this set is insufficient for universal computation. In boolean algebra, generates only affine (linear) functions. To achieve a Turing-complete, universal logic family, we fundamentally require a non-linear primitive: an AND gate or an OR gate.

Then comes the dramatic plot twist: neither an AND gate nor an OR gate can be constructed using boundary bonds of junctions alone.

To see why, consider a standard AND gate and imagine a simple feedback loop: if we tie its output back to one of its inputs, the remaining free input must still be capable of freely accepting either a "0" or a "1" while remaining topologically consistent.

Code 
# Initialize the schematic canvas
with schemdraw.Drawing() as d:
    d.config(fontsize=12, unit=2.5)

    # 1. Place the 2-input AND gate
    and_gate = d.add(logic.And().right())

    # 2. Top Input: Lead wire connected to label "X"
    d.add(
        elm.Line()
        .left(1.5)
        .at(and_gate.in1)
        .label("X", loc="left")
    )

    # 3. Output wire extending to the right
    out_wire = d.add(
        elm.Line()
        .right(1)
        .at(and_gate.out)
    )

    # 4. Feedback loop: wire routing from output back into the bottom input (in2)
    d.add(elm.Line().down(1).at(out_wire.end))
    d.add(elm.Line().left(3.6))
    d.add(elm.Wire("|-").to(and_gate.in2))  # Clean 90-degree landing into input 2

Within a conjugated junction, however, this flexibility collapses. The strict local valency constraints (exactly one -bond per carbon) force rigid correlations across the entire network. The boundary bonds cannot fluctuate independently; their states are frozen into rigid, complementary pairs—either locked at "0" or locked at "1". The network lacks the internal degree of freedom required to break symmetry.

In other words, imagine a black box with a single carbon bond sticking out (representing the input ‘X’ to our self-looped AND gate). Whatever molecular topology sits inside that box, it will only ever succeed in clamping that sticking bond to a fixed "0" or a fixed "1". Never both simultaneously. It cannot act as a truly independent, open-ended variable.

Because we already possess a functional NOT gate, the ability to construct an OR gate would immediately yield an AND gate via De Morgan’s laws:

The impossibility of constructing an AND gate therefore seals the fate of the OR gate as well. Neither can exist within these passive junctions, completely blocking our path toward a universal logic family.

This snag became a major roadblock — the kind of theoretical brick wall that stalls an investigation for months on end. Nature does not yield its computational secrets that easily!

A junction alone is too rigid, too linear. To break the deadlock, we must look beyond and introduce a new mechanism into the carbon backbone…

item.description:
“Truth is not a stone to be thrown. It is a river that polishes the rocks. Drink from it too quickly, and you will taste only sand.”
— Professor Alvin

Logical Systems

While we are most familiar with logic gates built using silicon transistors, there are many other fascinating ways to implement logical systems. These alternative substrates demonstrate that Boolean logic is fundamentally an abstract mathematical concept that can be embodied in countless physical forms, often in surprising and ingenious ways.
Here are a few notable examples:

Electromechanical Relays

Relays are electromechanical devices that use an electromagnet to physically open or close an electrical circuit. They were widely used in early computing machinery, such as early electromechanical Turing machines, to implement logic gates. Although slower and more prone to mechanical wear than transistors, relays were a pivotal milestone in the history of computer engineering.

Vacuum Tubes

Following relays, thermionic valves (vacuum tubes) became the dominant technology for constructing logic gates. Despite being bulky, fragile, and power-hungry, these devices played a crucial role in the birth of electronic computing, powering machines like ENIAC.

Mechanical Systems (Marbles, Gears)

Purely mechanical systems can be designed to represent binary states (for example, the physical position of a marble or the discrete rotation of a gear) and execute logical operations. While intrinsically slow, these systems offer a tactile, highly visual demonstration of computation.

  • Marble-based logic systems:

  • LEGO-based mechanisms:
  • Pulley and weight systems:

Fluidics (Water, Air)

Fluidic logic systems utilize liquids or gases to represent bits (such as the presence, absence, or pressure level of a fluid within a channel) to perform operations without moving mechanical parts. These setups are often used to demonstrate control logic in harsh, radiation-heavy environments or for intuitive educational models.

  • Water-based fluidic systems:

Optics (Lasers, Mirrors)

Optical computing leverages photons to represent bits and process information. By manipulating light beams through lasers, beam splitters, mirrors, and non-linear optical crystals, logic gates can theoretically operate at the speed of light with minimal heat dissipation.

  • Laser-based optical systems:

Unconventional Binary Substrates

Beyond these classical media, an almost limitless variety of physical systems can compute. Researchers have successfully implemented logic using plant root growth patterns, DNA strand displacement, engineered bacterial colonies, magnetic domain walls, and even swarms of soldier crabs.

“Computer Scientists Build Computer Using Swarms of Crabs”

Exploring these alternative substrates does more than broaden our intellectual appreciation of logic; it paves the way for technologies that could disrupt medicine, molecular robotics, distributed sensing, and environmental monitoring.
While many remain at the proof-of-concept stage, they stand as a testament to human ingenuity and our ability to rethink the physical foundations of computation.

Designing a Universal Physical Computer

Imagine we now want to create a computer using an entirely new physical substrate, capable of executing arbitrary algorithms. To achieve this, the system must not only implement a set of universal logic gates, but it must also satisfy rigorous operational criteria to function as a Turing-complete machine:

  • Physical State Representation: First and foremost, we must unambiguously define how Boolean states are physically encoded. The reliability of this encoding is vital to ensure deterministic, noise-resilient operations. In classical electronics, “0” and “1” correspond to low and high voltage thresholds; in a mechanical computer, they might correspond to the spatial coordinates of a marble or the angle of a latch.
  • Signal Propagation and Fan-out: The system must reliably transmit signals across space while minimizing dissipation and crosstalk. This requires an efficient transport mechanism capable of driving the output of one gate into the inputs of multiple subsequent gates (fan-out) without signal degradation. In electronics, this is achieved through metallic traces; in fluidics, via micro-channels; in optics, through waveguides or optical fibers.
  • State Retention and Control: Finally, a complete computational architecture demands memory (the ability to store intermediate states) and a control mechanism. Control ensures that operations occur in a well-defined sequence and that system states evolve coherently over time.

The Scaling Wall: From Silicon Transistors to Molecules

From an engineering standpoint, computational performance has historically been driven by scaling. To increase throughput and reduce latency, the prevailing strategy has been aggressive miniaturization—shrinking physical components to pack higher circuit densities onto a single die while boosting operating clock frequencies.

However, this scaling paradigm is now running into hard physical barriers. At the sub-nanometer scale, traditional silicon transistors run headlong into destructive quantum phenomena, such as parasitic electron tunneling and quantum interference, which trigger leakage currents and compromise deterministic switching. These effects, once negligible, now pose severe technical and thermodynamic bottlenecks.

Rather than treating quantum effects as adversaries to be suppressed, a radically different approach is to embrace and exploit them.

By harnessing quantum behavior natively, we can design computational architectures operating on fundamentally new principles. This paradigm shift leads directly to a compelling frontier: implementing computational logic at the molecular scale.

By turning quantum mechanics into an asset rather than an obstacle, this strategy marks a clean conceptual break from traditional computing. It reveals how Boolean logic, though classical in its abstract formulation, can be mapped onto domains where quantum mechanics governs the physical substrate—opening up entirely uncharted territories for the future of information processing.

Logical Gates

Basic logic gates are the elementary building blocks of any digital system. These gates are: NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR, XOR, and XNOR. Each gate exhibits a specific behavior, formally defined by a truth table that maps its inputs to its output.

The beauty of this representation is that functions can be chained together end-to-end using standard matrix multiplication.

Quantum computing operates through superpositions and probabilities — concepts that often feel deeply counterintuitive to a mind conditioned by binary logic.

Children, however, are entirely comfortable with a world where anything is possible, where something can simultaneously be “this” and “that,” much like a quantum state in superposition. In many ways, their cognitive style is far closer to the natural quantum fabric of reality.

That is why playful, hands-on experiences often provide the best entry point for truly grasping quantum computing — even for adults!

Game 4: How the Mystery Box Answers

  • A switch controls the thickness of a line. (for example: ‘OFF’ means ‘thin line’. ‘ON’ means ‘thick line’).

  • A light shows the thickness of a line. (for example: ‘thin line’ means ‘light OFF’. ‘thick line’ means ‘light ON’).

  • Choose how you want to set your switches. (for example: Top line is thick, bottom line is thin).

  • Identify all the drawings that match your pattern. If you can’t find any, you get no answer, try a different pattern.

  • If you find one matching drawing, look at the lines connected to the lights: that is the Box’s answer!

  • If you find more than one matching drawing: close your eyes and select randomly ONE of the matching drawings.

Game 5: What is the Mystery Box For?

  • Try every combination (for example: thin/thin, thin/thick, thick/thin, thick/thick). Note down the results.

  • The lines can stand for anything you want: a thick line on the left could mean: “Is it raining outside?”. A thick line on the right could answer: “Take an umbrella!”.

  • What could the box be used for ? Find something useful.

Game 6: Reverse Mystery !

  • What if you change the buttons into lights, and the lights into buttons?

  • Surprise ! The box also works in reverse !

  • You can run forward, ask a question to find an answer, or run backward, start with an answer to reveal a question that created it!

The Mystery Revealed: You Just Built a Quantum Computer

Now, it is time to reveal what you were actually doing with your pencil:

You were not just doodling on paper. You were simulating a Quantum Molecular Computer:

  1. The Dots are Carbon atoms.
  2. The thin and thick lines are single and double chemical bonds ( and bonds).
  3. The multiple drawings on your page are quantum superpositions of molecular resonance states.
  4. Landing your finger on one drawing with your eyes closed is a quantum measurement!
  5. Running the drawings backwards is reversible quantum computation!

With a little hands-on experimentation, you will quickly develop a solid intuitive grasp of how the mechanics work.

Quantum molecular computing may seem daunting at first glance, but at its core, it is governed by simple, deterministic rules—much like the constraints of a board game. You no longer have an excuse to claim that quantum mechanics is inherently too complicated or counterintuitive to comprehend!

However, it must be acknowledged that truly mastering the game remains a genuine challenge.

Two fundamental questions remain:

  • How do we build specific structures to achieve a desired computational outcome?
    and
  • What is the true computational power of quantum molecular systems?

“Out of the void arises matter, just as out of silence emerges an idea.”
— Professor Alvin

Welcome, Fellow Explorers!

Whether you are a seasoned quantum physicist, a curious software engineer, a student wandering through the fringes of the web, or simply someone fascinated by the architecture of reality: welcome aboard.

You have just stepped into an open laboratory dedicated to an unconventional scientific journey. Here, we step away from traditional silicon chips and ultra-cold cryostats to explore how the elegant, subtle geometry of conjugated carbon systems could form the backbone of a radically different kind of quantum processor. Make yourself comfortable, bring your curiosity, and let’s explore what happens when we look at matter through the lens of computation.

How I Work

The bulk of this research has been conducted over the years using nothing more than a simple graphite pencil and stacks of paper. I find it deeply amusing that the very same carbon atoms I smear across a sheet of paper might one day, if arranged with enough precision, form a quantum supercomputer.

This website is the digital transcription of my physical laboratory notebook, and I will continue adding new findings as time permits. It is an evolving work in progress.

Scientific inquiry consists of sudden bursts of euphoria followed by long, quiet stretches of rumination. Do not be discouraged if updates pause for long intervals; that downtime is simply the recharge cycle my neurons require before taking the next quantum leap.

A Disclaimer on the Speculation / Wild Thoughts Section

The creative phase of scientific discovery is often anything but strictly scientific. True inspiration can strike from the most unexpected corners of reality.

The Speculations section at the bottom of each article exists so I can think out loud without self-censorship. Any idea is welcome there, provided it has a conceptual thread connecting it to the topic at hand — and above all, the spark needed to ignite novel ways of thinking.

A fair warning: If your sensibilities are offended by free-form intuition that casually weaves rigorous science, spaghetti sauce, space aliens, and unicorns into the same conceptual thought experiment—skip that section entirely!

House Rules for Discussions & Feedback

You are warmly invited to comment, debate, and constructively critique any post. To keep this space constructive and enjoyable to read, please adhere to a single cardinal rule:

Ad hominem attacks are strictly forbidden. Ideas, however, can be attacked as fiercely and relentlessly as you wish.

Bring your sharpest arguments, not your personal grievances.

The Road Ahead

It is important to emphasize that the work presented across these notes remains firmly in the theoretical realm. While these concepts are explored with analytical depth, their real-world physical implementation will demand significant experimental and technological breakthroughs. Scaling and testing them will inevitably reveal growing layers of complexity, demanding both deep interdisciplinary synergy and sustained reflection.

And yet, despite all the underlying complexity… the fundamental rules are so strikingly intuitive that a five-year-old could grasp them without breaking a sweat.
